newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Fertiliser margins weigh on Norsk Hydro.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fertiliser margins weigh on Norsk Hydro.

text.p: Norway's largest listed company, Norsk Hydro said on Monday lower fertiliser margins and reduced retail gasoline sales together with higher financial expenses led to a 4.5 percent fall in first-half 1997 pre-tax profits, despite a rise in operating income.

The industrial giant booked profits before tax for the first six months of 5.87 billion crowns ($795 million), against 6.14 billion in the corresponding 1996 period. Operating profits amounted to 5.98 billion crowns, four percent up from 5.75 billion crowns.
Net financial charges rose to 405 million, compared with an income of 61 million crowns. Earnings per share were set at 13.30 crowns versus 14.40 crowns for the first half 1996.
Hydro attributed the improvement in operating income to increased earnings for oil and gas, light metals and petrochemicals. For agriculture, earnings declined, it said.
Egil Myklebust, Hydro's President and chief executive, said the figures confirmed the positive trend seen in the first quarter.
"The work to realise the growth strategies presented last year is on schedule and investments in the first half of the year totalled 5.7 billion crowns," Myklebust said in a statement.
"Several divisions have put into effect initiatives aimed at reducing costs, while other cost-reduction programmes are about to be introduced."

The results, although largely in line with expectations, depressed the company's share price in early trade on the Oslo bourse, but dealers said the move was exaggerated by generally weaker stock markets worldwide. At 1040 GMT Hydro's share stood 2.64 percent, or 10 crowns, off at 388 crowns.

"Hydro (results) was not great but it wasn't a disaster either," said an Oslo-based analyst. "We knew fertiliser prices had been dropping this year, so really we should have seen this coming. But the rest of the year could be tricky," he said.

Hydro's agriculture business posted a first-half operating income of 1.4 billion crowns against 1.76 billion crowns last year. The company said the 20 percent reduction was mainly due to a decline in prices for nitrogen fertilisers in Europe.

"It is not easy to say that the pressure on margins is temporary," Odd Gullberg, Hydro's chief spokesman, said at a news conference. "It is positive that we are maintaining volumes, but that also adds a cost to us."
Outside Europe, Hydro said fertiliser earnings were affected only slightly by weaker prices as well as by China's suspension of fertiliser imports.
Higher prices and lower depreciation costs helped the oil and gas division to an 18 percent upturn in operating income to 3.48 billion crowns from 2.95 billion crowns.

Operating profits in light metals rose seven percent to 1.06 billion crowns due to increased electricity generation and better earnings for aluminium semi-fabrication activites. A favourable dollar/crown exchange rate also help lift the result.

Hydro said it planned to start all idle aluminium production capacity in the third quarter and add additional output during the remainder of the year. Primary aluminium output is planned to reach 740,000 tonnes per year by the end of 1997, compared with 675,000 tonnes at the end of 1996.

"We have continued to start up extra production according to regulations and customers' needs," Thomas Knutzen, a spokesman for Hydro Aluminium, told Reuters. "We've had fairly strong demand from our customers and we reqire additional production to serve their needs."
Analysts said the light metals improvement would likely lead to an upgrade of estimates for the overall year.
"It will be interesting to see, however, how the start up of idle capacity will affect the (aluminium) market. I assume they have sound grounds to increase capacity," commented one analyst.

Operating income for petrochemicals almost doubled from the first half 1996 to 178 million crowns, versus 90 million crowns, mainly due to higher PVC prices and reduced maintenance costs. However, earnings were hit by lower caustic soda prices and an increase in raw material costs, Hydro said.
--Oslo newsroom, +47 22 42 50 41 ($ = 7.383 Norwegian Crowns)
